name: Devil's claw (Harpagophytum procumbens)
short: Case reports: low blood sodium (SIADH) that recurred on re-use, and high blood pressure. Review of 28 trials: in double-blind ones, adverse events no more common than placebo; more safety data needed.
text: A systematic review of the safety of Harpagophytum procumbens identified 28 clinical trials, 20 of which reported adverse events; in none of the double-blind studies were adverse events more common than with placebo, minor adverse events (mainly gastrointestinal) occurred in around 3% of patients, a few reports of acute toxicity were found but none of chronic toxicity, and the reviewers said more safety data are urgently needed because the dosage used in most of the studies was at the lower limit and long-term treatment with these products is, in their view, advisable. A separate review of 14 osteoarthritis studies said the assessment of safety is limited by the small populations studied and that devil's claw appears to carry minor risk relative to NSAIDs, with long-term assessment still required. A case report describes a 65-year-old woman with high blood pressure who twice developed hyponatraemia (low blood sodium) from the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) while taking it for osteoarthritis, the link being confirmed when it recurred after the herb was reintroduced; another case report, available only as a title, describes systemic hypertension induced by devil's claw. Interaction evidence is from laboratory studies only: commercial preparations inhibited, and on longer exposure increased, the drug transporter P-glycoprotein in a human kidney cell line, which the authors said raises the possibility of herb-drug interactions still to be explored, whereas a screen of 10 preparations found only weak effects on the drug-metabolising enzyme CYP3A4 and concluded they are unlikely to have a clinically relevant effect on CYP function. No interaction with a named medicine was reported in the cited sources.
